why: B keeps every fact while fixing the reading hazards: it says the downloaded zip is Consent-O-Matic's, defines the 30-minute rest before saying what earns it, and splits the browser-choice rule into sub-bullets; A is the tersest, refers to 'the rest' before defining it, and its 'pinned Chromium release zip' reads as a browser download.

why: All four keep the same thresholds; B reads the quality threshold out in words and keeps the compact ≤ notation for speed and reliability, C and D are identical and fine, and A's 'at least one ... on 95% of queries or more' is redundant and slower to parse.
The four versions are character-for-character identical, so the order is arbitrary.

D gives the stealth bullet a subject ('web-mcp uses ...') so all four bullets read as parallel failure scenarios; B and C are identical, and A's stray comma in 'fail, or hang' is the only difference that reads worse.
D names the actor ('The installer denies') and says plainly 'If the install fails'; A leaves 'they are denied' agentless and 'If that fails' with a vaguer antecedent.
C's 'from then on they are fixed' is the clearest statement that the query set is frozen after one skim; D's 'Thresholds Q1–Q3 as proposed are fixed' is awkward enough to make the reader reparse it.
A spells out that query, papers and max_passages are parameters and that engines/since are described in goal 8, which an outside reader needs; D is the same as C minus a comma.
A states the rule as a full sentence ('uses a fixed English locale') and then what it doesn't depend on; C's fragment 'English, fixed, for every engine' and dangling 'It' read slowest.

C turns the shorthand bullets into sentences that say what lives where and why the parsers test against captured pages; B keeps the awkward 'are parsers of what other tools write' and the terse 'Installer:' fragment.
